channel.title: The Epoch Institute — What's new
channel.description: What the Institute has added and changed.

item.title: Test yourself on paper
item.description: The questions at the foot of the profiles, the century pages and the reading paths now print as a worksheet: lettered answers, a line for the name, and the answer key with the reasons on a page of its own, for a quick check in class.

item.title: 147 more people placed in time
item.description: 147 people of the encyclopedia who had no dates now carry the years of their own deeds, from the Roman jurist Ulpian to the last bey of Titteri, so they appear on the people and century pages; and 19 more entries lost a picture of a namesake, among them the Han princess Liu Xijun, who had been shown as a present-day singer.

item.title: Read further on Wikipedia
item.description: Some 27,000 encyclopedia entries now link the Wikipedia article on the same subject, and its Wikidata item, each match checked by the picture, the years or the text rather than the name alone; entries dated to a day link that day in Today in History; and 25 entries lost a picture taken from a namesake, so the village of Kanye no longer shows Kanye West, nor the Mongol prince Duden the German dictionary.

item.title: Kpojito, paroikoi and propiska
item.description: 34 more encyclopedia entries for the ranks and words of the social ladders, from Dahomey's queen mother, the kpojito, and Byzantium's dependent peasants to the Heian regents, the Soviet propiska and special settlements, and coartación and Gracias al Sacar in Spanish America; and Allahverdi Khan, the Safavid general, no longer opens the page of a Bengal nawab.

item.title: Every song has its own picture
item.guid: 2026-11-07 Every song has its own picture
item.description: Each of the 406 songs now shares with a picture of its own: its title, its name in its own script and the first lines of its words with the English beside them; and two of the oldest songs, the Hymn to Ninkasi and the Kesh Temple Hymn, now print their Sumerian words and translation.

item.title: The daily games run to November 2027
item.guid: 2026-11-07 The daily games run to November 2027
item.description: Connections has 120 new puzzles, Who Said It? 707 new quotations, with 201 speakers new to the game, from Theodoric and Murasaki Shikibu to Booker T. Washington, and Six Degrees runs to the end of October 2027 too; and the picture credits of a few hundred pages read cleanly now.

item.title: Who was who on the social ladders
item.guid: 2026-11-07 Who was who on the social ladders
item.description: 266 new encyclopedia entries: the councils of Venice, the Heian court and its writers, the Gulag, the peoples and gods of Gaul, the temples of Angkor, the Ming secret police and many more names the social ladders mention, now shown on the ranks they belong to; the gods of the Yoruba religion, from Obatala and Shango to Oshun and Eshu, with pictures on its page; and Seneca the philosopher, no longer confused with the Seneca people.

item.title: Kings and queens told apart
item.description: Rulers who share a name are now linked to the right one when the year shows which is meant: Charles III on the United Kingdom page is the British king, not a prince of Monaco, and Afonso I of Portugal no longer opens the king of Kongo; the religion, culture and movement pages had their links checked too.

item.title: Gold links checked on every state and empire page
item.guid: 2026-11-06 Gold links checked on every state and empire page
item.description: Every gold link on the 507 state and empire profiles was audited: nearly 200 wrong links are gone (Gran Colombia no longer links Esztergom, Saint Louis is no longer a Bavarian duke, the caliph Abu Bakr is the caliph), names inside longer names no longer link on their own anywhere on the site, and the island of Samos has its own entry.

item.title: Kayaks, nuraghi and Dong Son drums
item.guid: 2026-11-06 Kayaks, nuraghi and Dong Son drums
item.description: Fifteen new encyclopedia entries on the things the early and living peoples made, from the kayak and the umiak to the nuraghi of Sardinia, the Clovis point, Japan's dogū figures and the bronze drums of Dong Son, now picture the Kids stories of the Inuit, the Thule, Clovis, Jōmon, Dong Son and six more peoples; and a new Picture Puzzle set, Machines and Inventions.

item.title: Ten more encyclopedia entries
item.description: McCarthyism, De-Stalinization, the Exodus, Hitler's rise to power, the Orange Revolution, the Hawaiian sovereignty movement, the proclamation of the People's Republic of China, the Meiji era, the Marquis de Lafayette and Joe Hill, each written from its source and linked where the site names them.

item.title: Social ladders by country, two new picture puzzles
item.guid: 2026-11-06 Social ladders by country, two new picture puzzles
item.description: Each country history now links the social ladders of the societies that lived there, from Old Babylonia and Han China to the Zulu Kingdom; and the Picture Puzzle has two new sets of twelve, Ships and Voyages (from the Oseberg ship to the Mayflower and the Bounty) and Statues and Sculpture (from the Mask of Agamemnon and the Lady of Elche to the Bamberg Horseman).

item.title: Speeches and songs, songs of each country
item.guid: 2026-11-06 Speeches and songs, songs of each country
item.description: A speech now lists the songs that name its speaker, and a song the speeches of the people it names (Luther, Gandhi, Lincoln, Mandela, Tagore, Mao and more); every country history lists its songs; and the search filters follow the corrected regions of the people.

item.title: Great works
item.description: A new kind of profile: twenty great works of writing and building, from the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Code of Hammurabi and the Great Pyramid of Giza to the Divine Comedy, the Popol Vuh, Angkor Wat, the churches of Lalibela, Machu Picchu and the Taj Mahal, each with how it was made, received, survived and remembered.

item.title: Picture stories for Kids
item.description: In Kids mode, every one of the 65 culture profiles now opens with a short picture story that the page can read aloud, from the Natufians and the Indus cities to the Inuit, the Māori and the San today; the Kids Corner lists them all.

item.title: People by region
item.description: Nine new pages of People in History, one for each region of the world, with the best known first and then century by century; and 1,252 people placed in their right region, checked against where they were born, died and worked.

item.title: Eighteen songs translated
item.description: Eighteen songs printed in their own words now have the Institute's English beside them, line by line, with romanizations for the Sanskrit, Tamil, Bengali, Odia, Greek and Japanese: among them the Bhaja Govindam, the Hymn of Kassiani, Funiculì, Funiculà, La Paloma and the anthems of Brazil, Portugal, Norway and Romania. Twenty-two songs whose lyrics come from Genius also offer its English translation.

item.title: Lyrics from Genius
item.description: Ninety-one songs whose words the Institute does not print, most of them still in copyright, now offer their lyrics from Genius: a button under The words opens Genius's own embed, shown under its licence. Nothing loads from Genius until you press it.

item.title: Easier to read, easier to use
item.guid: 2026-11-06 Easier to read, easier to use
item.description: An accessibility pass to the WCAG 2.2 AA standard: faint grey and gold labels are now drawn at full strength, links inside running text are underlined as well as coloured, maps that hold links read as groups of links to screen readers, small picture-credit links are easier to tap, and wide tables in the essays can be scrolled from the keyboard.

item.title: New daily game: Six Degrees
item.description: A new daily puzzle in History Games: get from one encyclopedia entry to another, from Cleopatra to the printing press, by following the gold links in each entry's description. Every click counts, and the shortest route is shown at the end. It joins the week's results in My Week of Games.

item.title: Four new essays, eight Kids themes, 208 game pictures
item.guid: 2026-11-05 Four new essays, eight Kids themes, 208 game pictures
item.description: Four new essays in the Research Series read the Institute's own collections side by side: Faiths on the Move (how thirty religions spread, met and ended), Who Invented It First? (what 291 inventions show about firsts and credit), From Ruler to Enslaved (fifty social ladders compared) and The Written Word (how thirty-two languages were written, carried and revived). The Kids Corner and Word Hunt have eight new themes, from the Mongols and the Silk Road to the Renaissance and the Industrial Revolution; the picture games have 208 new pictures, and the Picture Puzzle a new set, Great Buildings.

item.title: Social ladders: fifty societies
item.description: Ten more social ladders, fifty in all: Ming China, Kievan Rus' and the bondsmen of the Russkaya Pravda, the Khmer Empire at Angkor, Majapahit, the Delhi Sultanate under the Tughluqs, Aksum under Ezana, the Zulu Kingdom, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, the Dutch Republic in its Golden Age and British India around 1900. Every rank has its picture, its estimated share and the way in and out of it.

item.title: Ten more social ladders
item.description: Ten more societies set out rank by rank, from ruler to enslaved: Qing China and Heian Japan, Ayutthaya under the sakdina system, Safavid Iran, Ptolemaic Egypt, Gaul before Caesar, the Asante Empire and the Kingdom of Dahomey, the Republic of Venice and the Soviet Union under Stalin. Each has its estimated shares, how people rose and fell, the place of women, a picture for every rank, and a chance to be born into it.

item.title: Songs in History: 67 more
item.description: Sixty-seven more songs, 406 in all: the Song of Songs, Psalm 104, the Hallel and the Song of Hannah, the Hymn to the Nile, the Tevaram, the Charyapada and the Bhaja Govindam, the anthems of Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco, Thailand, Uganda and Gujarat, Sari Gelin and Ya Mustafa, Sweet Mother and Meadowlands, the Queen's Prayer and Tinsagu nu Hana, spirituals, sea shanties and carols, and favourites from Funiculì, Funiculà to Take Me Out to the Ball Game. Each has its story, a performance, and, where they are free to print, its words.

item.title: Which came first: cultures and ideas
item.guid: 2026-11-04 Which came first: cultures and ideas
item.description: Which Came First? now has a round of its own for the cultures, movements, ideologies, religions and languages: did the Etruscans come before Daoism, or the Bauhaus before Romanticism? A tap on the map of a country history now shows which states had their seat near that spot, the atlas lists the songs of a country beside its states, and a new page, My Week of Games, sets your last seven days of the daily games side by side. And two long essays of the Research Series, Before the State and How Songs Travel, are a quarter shorter.

item.title: 38 more Songs in History
item.description: 339 songs now: the Ballad of Mulan, the Epic of Sundiata, the Song of Deborah and the Enūma Eliš; Byzantine hymns of Kassia and the Akathist; Ma'oz Tzur, Victimae paschali laudes, In dulci jubilo, Gaudete and Es ist ein Ros entsprungen; the anthems of Brazil, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Romania, the Czech lands, Wales, Portugal and Odisha; the songs of the Ghost Dance, Joshua Fit the Battle of Jericho, Saint Louis Blues and Solidarity Forever; Molly Malone, Drunken Sailor, Loch Lomond, The Three Ravens, Men of Harlech and Malbrough. 31 with their words in the original, many with an English translation, and a performance for 37.

item.title: Today's Number, a dice for surprises, and a play button
item.guid: 2026-11-04 Today's Number, a dice for surprises, and a play button
item.description: The home page now shows a number a day from the data, with the page it comes from, and the Song of the Day plays where it stands. A dice in the header leaps to a random page of history. Reading paths print as a booklet, year pages now start at four things to read (162 more years), and the menu names the States Register and the Power Curves.

item.title: 463 more links in the state histories
item.guid: 2026-11-04 463 more links in the state histories
item.description: The histories of 390 states now link the encyclopedia entries added since they were written: the forms of government (chiefdom, oligarchy, absolute monarchy, one-party state), the fiefs of Europe's counties and duchies, the Bolsheviks, caciques and zamindars, Mycenae, Knossos and the Maya cities, the turtle ships of Joseon and the waterwheels of Hama. Cannon now has links of its own across the site. Encyclopedia entries now link their full profile, and the profiles list the Research Series essays that discuss them.

item.title: 73 more inventions and discoveries
item.description: The inventions tree now holds 291, most of them in the lanes that were thin: the sewing needle of Denisova Cave, farming at Kuk Swamp, wine, cheese and coffee, fired brick, Egyptian blue and lacquerware, the shadoof, the water clock, the sundial, the screw and the lathe, Zhang Heng's seismoscope, the wheelbarrow, the kite and the junk, the pencil, the barometer and the thermometer, canning, the stethoscope and blood transfusion, Morse code, Braille and the phonograph, the electric motor, alternating current, hydroelectricity, radar, the personal computer and the lithium-ion battery, each with its own encyclopedia entry.

item.title: 35 more Great Speeches
item.description: 115 speeches now, from King Wu of Zhou at Muye to Lyndon B. Johnson's "We shall overcome": Alcibiades for the Sicilian expedition, Cato on the Oppian law, Caesar on the Catilinarians, al-Hajjaj at Kufa, Richard II at Smithfield, Powhatan to John Smith, Galileo's abjuration, Logan's Lament, Burke for conciliation with America and against Warren Hastings, Robert Emmet from the dock, Chief Seattle, the House Divided, John Brown to the court, Itō Hirobumi's rising sun, Tagore on nationalism, Pearse at O'Donovan Rossa's grave, the Four Freedoms and the Marshall Plan. 31 with their full text, and new entries for 14 of their speakers.

item.title: 557 more events in Today in History
item.guid: 2026-11-04 557 more events in Today in History
item.description: Every day of the year now has more to read: 3,679 events in all, among them the Battle of Badr, the Council of Nicaea, the Mongols at the walls of Kaifeng, the Coonan Cross Oath, the fall of Ayutthaya, Yi Sun-sin at Myeongnyang, the Treaty of Karlowitz, Dandara of Palmares and the Stockholm Bloodbath. Each is dated by the text of its own source.

item.title: 24 new reading paths
item.description: Sixty-two paths now: new routes through the ideologies and forms of government, abolition and votes for women, living peoples and the cultures before the state, the ancient gods and the faiths of Persia, the ancient Near East, Mesoamerica and the Andes, West, East and Southern Africa, the Mongol world, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia, the Ottomans and Russia, the nations of the nineteenth century and the inventions that changed the world.

item.title: 921 more quotations for Who Said It?
item.guid: 2026-11-04 921 more quotations for Who Said It?
item.description: Who Said It? now runs to July 2027 without a repeat: 1,247 quotations from 343 people, among them Sappho and Pindar, Qu Yuan and Emperor Taizong, Ibn Arabi and Kabir, Anselm and Marlowe, Mary Wollstonecraft, Olaudah Equiano, Frederick Douglass, Susan B. Anthony and Sol Plaatje. Every quotation is copied from a public-domain text, never typed.

item.title: 120 more History Connections puzzles
item.description: Daily Connections now runs to the first of July 2027: 120 new puzzles from every region and age, from the Kings of Rome and the Khagans of the Göktürks to the Obas of Benin, the Māori King movement and the hidden words of Hide a vegetable.

item.title: 111 more encyclopedia entries, and dates for 67 events
item.guid: 2026-11-04 111 more encyclopedia entries, and dates for 67 events
item.description: The composers, singers and writers behind Songs in History, from Josquin, Palestrina and Purcell to Paul Robeson, Pete Seeger, Miriam Makeba, Umm Kulthum, Lata Mangeshkar and Kazi Nazrul Islam; the revolutions of 1848 and the division of Korea; and the last names of the social ladders: the nobles of the robe and of the sword, lettres de cachet, the kisaeng and chungin of Joseon, the Byzantine tagmata, the Spartan mothakes and the conspiracy of Cinadon, the Khongirad and the Radhanites. Sixty-seven great events that had no dates now have them, from the Punic Wars and the Greco-Persian Wars to Waterloo and both world wars, so they stand on their century and year pages.

item.title: 184 more encyclopedia entries
item.description: The ranks, offices and people the social ladders named: the Abbasid jurists Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʻi and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the Mihna; the askeri, the Enderun School and Hürrem Sultan; the taille, the gabelle, Turgot, Necker and the Women’s March on Versailles; the affranchis, Bois Caïman and Dutty Boukman; the gwageo, the hopae and the sangmin; the kuge, the hatamoto and the rōnin; the hersir, the housecarls and the Thing; Li Qingzhao, Fan Zhongyan and Ouyang Xiu; Kamehameha II and the ʻAi Noa.

item.title: 137 more encyclopedia entries
item.description: Ancient Egypt, Greece, the Maya, the Inca, the Aztecs and Hawaii as the social ladders describe them: Tutankhamun, Nefertari, the Valley of the Kings and Deir el-Medina; Athenian democracy, the boule, the agoge and Cynisca; Copán, Palenque and Calakmul; the calmecac, the mitma and the kapu. With them the people and works the profiles named: Claude Monet, Bertrand Russell, Rashi, Hildegard of Bingen, Thomas Becket, Ban Zhao, the Book of Han, the Manusmriti, the Great Purge and the Ten Commandments.

item.title: 107 new encyclopedia entries
item.description: The subjects the profiles and speeches named but the encyclopedia lacked: Friedrich Engels, Harry S. Truman, Willy Brandt, Thomas More, Max Weber, Hannah Arendt, Rosa Luxemburg and Sayyid Qutb; the Paris Commune, the Nika riots, the Investiture Controversy and the July Revolution; the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Talmud, the Guru Granth Sahib and The Spirit of the Laws; the Muslim Brotherhood, the Bolsheviks and Young Italy; and many more, each written from its source and linked from the profiles that name it.

item.title: Ideologies: a new kind of profile
item.guid: 2026-11-03 Ideologies: a new kind of profile
item.description: Twenty ideologies, each with its origins, core ideas, spread and variants, its record in power, the critiques made of it and its legacy: liberalism, conservatism, republicanism and nationalism; capitalism, mercantilism and imperialism; socialism, communism, anarchism, social democracy and Maoism; fascism; Legalism in ancient China; Kemalism, pan-Arabism, Hindutva, Islamism and Peronism; and feminism. Drawn from saved sources and checked line by line, with what was done in each one’s name stated plainly.

item.title: Twenty more movements
item.description: Twenty movements, reforms and revolutions: the Counter-Reformation, Chartism, the Luddites and the Decembrists, Impressionism, Modernism and the Bauhaus, Solidarity, the Velvet Revolution and the environmental movement, the Taiping Rebellion, the May Fourth Movement, the Meiji Restoration and the Tanzimat, the Young Turks, Zionism and the Arab Spring, the Harlem Renaissance, Négritude and the Non-Aligned Movement.

item.title: Twelve more religions and sixteen more languages
item.guid: 2026-11-03 Twelve more religions and sixteen more languages
item.description: Twelve religions with their spread on the faith maps: the religions of Mesopotamia, Canaan, Rome and the Celts, Slavic paganism and Mithraism, Tengrism, Bon and Chinese folk religion, and the Druze faith, Yazidism and Haitian Vodou. And sixteen languages: Pali, Tamil, Malay, Mongolian, Armenian, Georgian, Middle Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Old English, Gothic, Old Church Slavonic, Phoenician, Coptic, Ge'ez, Guarani and Hawaiian.

item.title: Twenty more cultures
item.description: Profiles of twenty more peoples and cultures without a state of their own: living peoples (the San, Khoekhoe and Tuareg, the Inuit, Navajo, Lakota and Kalinago, and Aboriginal Australians) and the cultures known from archaeology, from the Clovis and Paracas cultures to La Tène, Hallstatt, Cucuteni–Trypillia, the Nuragic civilisation and the Iberians, and in Asia the Tocharians, Longshan, Hongshan, Erlitou and the Hoabinhian.

item.title: Eighty-one more state profiles
item.description: Full profiles, with power curves, key facts, section pictures and gold links, for 81 more states of the register: from Ur, Lagash and the Old Kingdom of Egypt to the Qin, Sui and Northern Wei, the Huns, Hephthalites and Uyghurs, Phrygia, Colchis and Artaxiad Armenia, the Visigoths, Vandals and Great Moravia, the Aghlabids, Idrisids, Marinids and Zengids, Funan, Chenla, Champa, Medang and Malacca, Ife, Dagbon, Loango, Ifat and Alodia, Saint-Domingue, Colonial Brazil, the Republic of Texas and the Confederacy, and the modern republics from Hungary and Turkey to Rwanda, Singapore and East Timor.

item.title: Two new essays: Before the State, and How Songs Travel
item.guid: 2026-11-02 Two new essays: Before the State, and How Songs Travel
item.description: Research Series 07 asks how peoples lived without kings, from the Natufians and the Jōmon to the five living cultures that have outlived the states around them; 08 follows the 300 songs of Songs in History from the oldest tablets to the anthems, the tunes that branched into other nations' songs, and what states and movements made of them. Also new in Songs in History: Chollima on the Wing, the song of North Korea's Chollima Movement, and an entry for the movement itself.

item.title: Songs of states and causes, and a dozen new features
item.guid: 2026-11-02 Songs of states and causes, and a dozen new features
item.description: Sixty-six songs of states, parties and causes join Songs in History, from Rule, Britannia! and the Soviet anthem to the songs of Mao's China, North Korea, fascist Italy and the Hong Kong protests, each told as history. New: compare any two profiles side by side; a timeline view of the profiles; Where Is This Song From?, a daily song game; Born on This Day on the home page; Next to read; search inside the songs' words; the encyclopedia filtered by era and by picture; levels in My Passport; an On This Day card for other websites; reading paths read aloud as a guided tour; this What's new page; worksheets on the cultures and the songs; and the Epic of Gilgamesh now in Sumerian.

item.title: Encyclopedia, offline reading, Meanwhile in the world
item.guid: 2026-11-02 Encyclopedia, offline reading, Meanwhile in the world
item.description: 229 songs and 16 forms of government have entries of their own; entries and songs show what else was happening in the world that year; the home page has a Song of the Day; pages already read open without a connection, and the site can be added to a phone's home screen.

item.title: Thirty new cultures
item.description: The culture archive grows from 15 to 45, with more of Asia and South Asia: Mehrgarh, the Vedic civilisation, Sangam-age Tamilakam, Jōmon, Yayoi, Liangzhu, Sanxingdui, Dong Son, the Ainu and more, from the Natufians and the Yamnaya to the Taíno, the Thule people and the Māori.

item.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh, and better performances
item.guid: 2026-11-02 The Epic of Gilgamesh, and better performances
item.description: The Epic of Gilgamesh joins Songs in History with Peter Pringle's performance in Sumerian; eight songs have a better recording.

item.title: Songs in History
item.description: 233 songs handed down through history, from a Sumerian hymn to songs of the Cold War: their story, their words in the original, romanized and in English where they are in the public domain, and a sung performance.

item.title: Forms of government
item.description: Twenty forms of government, from absolute monarchy to the city-state and colonial rule, each with how it works, its history, its strengths and weaknesses; a hub that compares them and lets you design a state; and an essay, Who Should Rule?

item.title: The inventions tree
item.description: 218 inventions and discoveries in eleven lanes, from stone tools to the World Wide Web: what each built on, what it led to and who made it first.

item.title: Social ladders
item.description: How thirty societies ranked their people, ruler to enslaved, with how many stood on each rung; be born into one by chance, compare two, or put the ranks in order in a game.

item.title: Thirty cultures and movements, speeches and paths
item.guid: 2026-10-29 Thirty cultures and movements, speeches and paths
item.description: The first cultures and movements, 138 new encyclopedia entries, twenty more great speeches and ten more reading paths.

item.title: Rise and Fall Race, Flashcards, Who Said It?
item.guid: 2026-10-28 Rise and Fall Race, Flashcards, Who Said It?
item.description: Race empires through the centuries, learn with flashcards, guess who said a quotation, test yourself at the end of a profile, and see everything you have read on My timeline.
